paragraphs.text: Mozzillo et al. (2014) reported a 22-year-old Italian woman (FS) who had had recurrent bleeding upper intestinal ulcers since age 5 years. She also had intestinal malrotation, partial duodenal intussusception, slow intestinal transit, and entero-gastric bile reflux. Her eye findings included reduced visual acuity, dyschromatopsia, optic disc pallor, and visual field defects, which were consistent with optic neuropathy. She did not have optic atrophy, and her pattern visual evoked potentials were normal. She had non-autoimmune, insulin-treated diabetes mellitus. She also had bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss with tinnitus triggered by loud environments. Her platelets showed defective aggregation to ADP and no secretion in response to ADP, but aggregation to collagen was normal. At age 22 years, she had diabetes mellitus, optic neuropathy with preserved visual acuity and normal electrophysiologic tests, no optic atrophy, tinnitus, bile reflux, slow intestinal transit, a reduced and reversible ADP platelet aggregation defect, and bleeding upper intestinal ulcers. Mozzillo et al. (2014) noted that their patient had optic neuropathy rather than optic atrophy, and that platelet aggregation was impaired to ADP rather than to collagen. They proposed that the eye disease in the Jordanian patients might also have been optic neuropathy. They suggested that so-called WFS2 might not be a subtype of Wolfram syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Amr et al. (2007) studied 3 consanguineous Jordanian families with WFS2. They found a homozygous G-to-C transversion at nucleotide 109 in a novel, highly conserved zinc-finger gene, ZCD2 (CISD2). The change predicts a glu37-to-gln (E37Q) substitution. Although the change is nonsynonymous at a conserved residue, the authors found that it was pathogenic because it disrupted mRNA splicing, removing exon 2 and introducing a premature stop codon. The encoded protein, which they named ERIS (endoplasmic reticulum intermembrane small protein), localized to the endoplasmic reticulum but did not interact directly with wolframin. Amr et al. (2007) found no mutations in the WFS2 gene in 377 probands with hearing loss.

paragraphs.text: In an Italian woman with WFS2, Mozzillo et al. (2014) sequenced CISD2 cDNA and found a novel homozygous deletion of the whole of exon 2. Using SNP array and PCR, they mapped the deletion to a maximum size of 2,050 bp. The deleted region included the codons for amino acids 102 to 106 within the 2Fe-2S domain, and the authors suggested that this could result in a nonfunctional protein. Her parents and brother were heterozygous carriers. The parents denied consanguinity, and runs of homozygosity did not show a relationship. However, microsatellite analysis supported a common ancestor, and the grandparents had been born on the same small Italian island.

paragraphs.text: In an Italian woman with Wolfram syndrome 2, Mozzillo et al. (2014) found a homozygous deletion of the whole of exon 2 of the CISD2 gene. Her features included diabetes mellitus, optic neuropathy without optic atrophy, recurrent bleeding upper intestinal ulcers, high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, and defective platelet aggregation to ADP. The deletion was at most 2,050 bp in size and removed the codons for amino acids 102 to 106 in the 2Fe-2S domain. Her parents and brother were heterozygous carriers. They had no diabetes, eye abnormalities, or deafness, but they did have a reversible ADP-induced platelet aggregation defect. Microsatellite analysis supported a common ancestor.
